q:
Allyl alcohol, CH2=CHCH2OH, is shown. Which statements about it are true?
I. It contains a hydroxyl (–OH) group.
II. All three carbon atoms have tetrahedral (109.5°) geometry.
III. Its molecular formula is C3H6O.
h: Count the electron groups around each carbon, then count every H, including the one on oxygen.
w: I and III only. I is true: the –OH on the end carbon is a hydroxyl group, so this is an alcohol. II is false: the two C=C carbons each have three electron groups and are trigonal planar (about 120°); only the CH2OH carbon is tetrahedral. III is true: there are 3 C, 6 H (2 + 1 + 2 on carbon and 1 on oxygen) and 1 O.
x: Statement III is true. Count the H atoms: 2 + 1 + 2 on the carbons plus 1 on the oxygen gives six.
Statement II is false. Each carbon of the C=C double bond has three electron groups, so it is trigonal planar, not tetrahedral.
Statement I is true. The –OH on the end carbon is a hydroxyl group, which makes this compound an alcohol.

q:
Which statements about the alkene shown are true?
I. Its IUPAC name is 2-methyl-2-butene.
II. It can exist as cis and trans isomers.
III. Its molecular formula is C5H12.
h: For cis–trans isomers, each C=C carbon needs two different groups. An alkene has two fewer H atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbons.
w: I only. I is true: the longest chain with the C=C has four carbons, numbered so the double bond starts at C2, and the methyl group is on C2. II is false: one C=C carbon holds two identical CH3 groups, so cis and trans forms cannot exist. III is false: a five-carbon alkene with one C=C is C5H10; C5H12 is the formula of the saturated alkanes.
x: Statement II is false. One carbon of the double bond carries two identical CH₃ groups, so swapping sides gives the same molecule.
Statement III is false. C₅H₁₂ is the formula of a saturated alkane. The C=C double bond means two fewer H atoms.
Statement II is false. A C=C carbon with two identical groups cannot give cis and trans forms.

q: Which of compounds I–III are aromatic?
h: At this level, an aromatic compound contains a benzene ring: six ring carbons joined by three alternating double bonds.
w: II only. Toluene (II) is a benzene ring with a methyl group, so it is aromatic. Cyclohexene (I) has one C=C, and 1,3-cyclohexadiene (III) has two C=C bonds plus a CH2 in the ring, so neither has the benzene ring of three alternating double bonds. I and III react like ordinary alkenes.
x: Compound III has two C=C bonds in a six-membered ring, but one ring carbon is a CH₂, so the ring is not a benzene ring.
Compound I is a cycloalkene. One C=C double bond in a ring does not make a benzene ring.
Compound III is not aromatic. A ring needs three alternating double bonds, and III has only two.

q: Which of alcohols I–III are secondary (2°)?
h: Find the carbon that holds the –OH, then count how many other carbons are bonded directly to that carbon.
w: II and III only. In cyclohexanol (II) the –OH carbon is bonded to two ring carbons, and in 2-butanol (III) it is bonded to a CH3 and a CH2, so both are 2°. In 2-methyl-2-propanol (I) the –OH carbon is bonded to three CH3 groups, so it is tertiary (3°).
x: Alcohol II is also secondary. The ring carbon that holds the –OH is bonded to two other ring carbons.
Alcohol I is tertiary. Its –OH carbon is bonded to three other carbons.
Alcohol I is not secondary. Count the carbons bonded to its –OH carbon and you get three.

q:
Which statements about aldehydes and ketones are true?
I. In a ketone, the C=O carbon is at the end of the carbon chain.
II. Propanal boils at a higher temperature than 1-propanol because aldehyde molecules hydrogen bond to each other.
III. Reducing propanone (adding H2) gives 2-propanol.
h: Recall where the C=O sits in an aldehyde versus a ketone, and which group lets molecules hydrogen bond to each other.
w: III only. I is false: the C=O carbon of a ketone is bonded to two carbons, so it sits inside the chain; an end-of-chain C=O bonded to H is an aldehyde. II is false: propanal has no O–H, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other, and it boils lower (48 °C) than 1-propanol (97 °C). III is true: reducing a ketone gives a secondary alcohol, and propanone gives 2-propanol.
x: Statement II is false. An aldehyde has no H on oxygen, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other, and 1-propanol boils higher.
Statement I is false. A C=O at the end of a chain, bonded to an H, is an aldehyde. A ketone's C=O carbon is bonded to two carbons.
Statement II is false. Without an O–H, aldehyde molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other.

q: Glycerol (I), 2-bromobutane (II) and alanine (III) are shown. Which of them contain a chiral carbon?
h: A chiral carbon has four different groups attached. Check carefully whether two groups on a carbon are really the same.
w: II and III only. In 2-bromobutane (II), C2 bears H, Br, CH3 and CH2CH3; in alanine (III), the α carbon bears H, NH2, CH3 and COOH. Glycerol (I) has no chiral carbon: its middle carbon bears H, OH and two identical CH2OH groups, and each end carbon has two H atoms.
x: Glycerol (I) is not chiral. Its middle carbon carries two identical –CH₂OH groups.
Molecule II also has a chiral carbon. C2 holds H, Br, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃, four different groups.
Glycerol (I) has no carbon with four different groups. The middle carbon has two identical CH₂OH groups.

q:
Acetic acid and methyl acetate are shown. Which statements are true?
I. Acetic acid is a weak acid that is only partly ionized in water.
II. At the body's pH of 7.4, acetic acid exists mainly as un-ionized CH3COOH.
III. Acetic acid boils at a higher temperature than methyl acetate because acetic acid molecules hydrogen bond to each other.
h: Carboxylic acids lose H<sup>+</sup> in solutions that are much less acidic than the acid itself. Esters have no O–H.
w: I and III only. I is true: acetic acid is a weak acid, so only a small fraction of its molecules ionize in water. II is false: pH 7.4 is far less acidic than acetic acid's pKa (about 4.8), so nearly all of it is present as the acetate ion, CH3COO−. III is true: acetic acid (118 °C) has an O–H and hydrogen bonds to itself, while methyl acetate (57 °C) has no O–H.
x: Statement III is true. Acetic acid has an O–H and hydrogen bonds to itself, while methyl acetate has no O–H.
Statement II is false. At pH 7.4, well above acetic acid's pKa of about 4.8, nearly all of it is ionized as acetate.
Statement II is false. In the near-neutral pH of the body a carboxylic acid loses its H⁺ and exists mainly as the carboxylate ion.

q: Which of amines I–III are secondary (2°)?
h: For amines, count the carbon groups bonded directly to the nitrogen (not to a carbon, as you do for alcohols).
w: II only. Amines are classified by the number of carbon groups on N. Propylamine (I) has one (1°), ethylmethylamine (II) has two (2°) and trimethylamine (III) has three (3°). Only II is secondary.
x: Amine III is tertiary. Its nitrogen is bonded to three carbon groups and has no N–H.
Amine I is primary. Its nitrogen is bonded to only one carbon, the end of the propyl chain.
Amine III is tertiary, not secondary. Count the carbon groups on its nitrogen and you get three.

q:
Which statements about monosaccharides and disaccharides are true?
I. Glucose and galactose differ only in the orientation of the –OH on one carbon (C4).
II. Sucrose is a reducing sugar.
III. Fructose is an aldohexose.
h: Ask which sugars have a free anomeric carbon that can open to a C=O, and where the C=O sits in open-chain fructose.
w: I only. I is true: glucose and galactose are both aldohexoses that differ only at C4. II is false: sucrose joins glucose C1 to fructose C2, so neither ring can open, and sucrose does not react with Benedict's reagent. III is false: fructose has its C=O at C2, a ketone, so it is a ketohexose.
x: Statement II is false. In sucrose both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond, so it cannot open and reduce Benedict's reagent.
Statement III is false. Fructose has a ketone group at C2, so it is a ketohexose.
Statement I is true. Glucose and galactose are both aldohexoses that differ only at C4.

q:
Which statements about polysaccharides are true?
I. Amylose and cellulose are both polymers of glucose.
II. Humans can digest cellulose because its glucose units are joined by α(1→4) glycosidic bonds.
III. Glycogen is more highly branched than amylopectin.
h: Compare the type of glycosidic link (α or β) in starch and cellulose, and how often each storage polymer branches.
w: I and III only. I is true: amylose and cellulose are both unbranched chains of glucose. II is false: cellulose's glucose units are joined by β(1→4) links, which human enzymes cannot hydrolyze, so cellulose passes through as fiber. III is true: glycogen branches about every 8–12 glucose units, more often than amylopectin (about every 24–30).
x: Statement III is true. Glycogen branches about every 8 to 12 glucose units, more often than amylopectin does.
Statement II is false. Cellulose has β(1→4) links, and human enzymes cannot break them.
Statement II is false. Humans lack an enzyme for the β(1→4) links in cellulose, so cellulose passes through as fiber.

q:
Which statements about fats and oils are true?
I. Vegetable oils are liquid at room temperature mainly because cis double bonds put kinks in their fatty acid chains.
II. Hydrogenating an oil adds H2 to C=C bonds and raises its melting point.
III. Cholesterol is a triacylglycerol.
h: Think about how chain shape affects how closely molecules pack, and what a triacylglycerol is built from.
w: I and II only. I is true: cis double bonds bend the chains, so oil molecules pack loosely and melt below room temperature. II is true: hydrogenation removes C=C bonds, the straighter chains pack better, and the melting point rises (oil becomes a soft solid such as margarine). III is false: cholesterol is a steroid with four fused rings, not glycerol esterified to three fatty acids.
x: Statement II is true. Adding H₂ removes C=C bonds, the straighter chains pack better, and the fat melts at a higher temperature.
Statement III is false. Cholesterol is a steroid with four fused rings, not glycerol joined to three fatty acids.
Statement III is false. Cholesterol has a fused four-ring steroid skeleton, not a glycerol backbone with fatty acids.

q:
Rank the fatty acids from lowest to highest melting point.
I. stearic acid: 18 carbons, saturated
II. oleic acid: 18 carbons, one cis C=C
III. palmitic acid: 16 carbons, saturated
h: A cis double bond kinks the chain and spoils packing. Among saturated chains, a longer chain has more dispersion forces.
w: II < III < I. Oleic acid (II) melts lowest (about 13 °C) because its cis double bond kinks the chain and prevents close packing. Of the two saturated acids, the longer stearic acid (I, about 69 °C) has more dispersion forces and melts higher than palmitic acid (III, about 63 °C).
x: This order puts oleic acid highest. A cis C=C bends the chain, so the molecules pack poorly and melt at a lower temperature, not a higher one.
Palmitic acid is placed above stearic acid here. Among saturated fatty acids, the longer chain has more dispersion forces and melts higher.
Palmitic acid is placed below oleic acid here. The cis kink lowers the melting point much more than removing two carbons does.

q:
Which statements about protein structure are true?
I. Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
II. The α-helix and β-pleated sheet are held mainly by hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups.
III. Heating a protein until it denatures breaks its peptide bonds.
h: Denaturation unfolds a protein. Ask which levels of structure depend on weak attractions and which on covalent bonds.
w: I and II only. I is true: the order of amino acids linked by peptide (amide) bonds is the primary structure. II is true: secondary structures form when backbone C=O groups hydrogen bond to backbone N–H groups. III is false: heat disrupts hydrogen bonds and other attractions that hold the folded shape, but the covalent peptide bonds stay intact, so the primary structure survives.
x: Statement II is true. The C=O of one amino acid hydrogen bonds to the N–H of another along the backbone in both helices and sheets.
Statement I is true. The order of amino acids, linked by peptide bonds, is the primary structure.
Statement III is false. Heat disrupts hydrogen bonds and other attractions, but the covalent peptide bonds stay intact.

q:
A human enzyme catalyzes a reaction at 37 °C when the substrate concentration is low. Which changes would increase the reaction rate?
I. Heating the mixture to 80 °C
II. Adding more enzyme
III. Adding more substrate
h: At low substrate concentration many active sites are empty. Think about what very high temperature does to a protein's shape.
w: II and III only. I is false: at 80 °C a human enzyme denatures, its active site loses its shape, and the rate drops. II is true: more enzyme means more active sites working at once. III is true: at low substrate concentration the active sites are not saturated, so more substrate means more enzyme–substrate complexes per second.
x: Change II also raises the rate. More enzyme molecules means more active sites working at once.
Change I does not raise the rate. A human enzyme denatures well below 80 °C and its active site loses its shape.
Change I lowers the rate. At 80 °C a human enzyme denatures.

q:
Which statements about nucleic acids are true?
I. DNA contains the sugar deoxyribose, while RNA contains ribose.
II. A G–C base pair is held by three hydrogen bonds, while an A–T pair is held by two.
III. Each nucleotide contains a nitrogen base, a five-carbon sugar and a phosphate group.
h: Recall the three parts of a nucleotide, how the two sugars differ, and how many hydrogen bonds each base pair forms.
w: I, II and III. I is true: RNA's ribose has an –OH on C2′, where DNA's deoxyribose has only H. II is true: G and C share three hydrogen bonds and A and T share two, so G–C rich DNA is harder to separate. III is true: a nucleotide is a base joined to a pentose sugar that carries a phosphate group.
x: Statement II is true. G and C are joined by three hydrogen bonds and A and T by two.
Statement I is true. RNA's ribose has an –OH on C2′ where DNA's deoxyribose has only an H.
Statement III is true. A nucleotide is a nitrogen base, a five-carbon sugar and a phosphate joined together.

q:
Which statements about glycolysis are true?
I. Glycolysis requires O2.
II. Glycolysis takes place in the mitochondrial matrix.
III. Glycolysis converts one glucose into two pyruvate with a net gain of 2 ATP.
h: Glycolysis is the first stage of glucose breakdown and also runs in cells working without enough oxygen.
w: III only. I is false: glycolysis is anaerobic and runs with or without O2, which is why muscles can make lactate during hard exercise. II is false: glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm; the citric acid cycle is the stage in the mitochondrial matrix. III is true: one six-carbon glucose gives two three-carbon pyruvate, with 4 ATP made and 2 used, a net of 2 ATP (plus 2 NADH).
x: Statement I is false. Glycolysis runs with or without oxygen, which is why muscles can make lactate during hard exercise.
Statement II is false. Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm. The citric acid cycle is the stage in the mitochondrial matrix.
Statement I is false. Glycolysis does not use O₂ at any step.

q:
Rank by the number of ATP produced when each is fully oxidized through the citric acid cycle and electron transport chain, from fewest to most.
I. one NADH
II. one FADH2
III. one acetyl CoA
h: FADH<sub>2</sub> passes its electrons in after complex I. One turn of the citric acid cycle makes several reduced coenzymes.
w: II < I < III. Using about 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2, FADH2 (II) gives fewer ATP than NADH (I) because its electrons enter at coenzyme Q and skip complex I's proton pumping. One acetyl CoA (III) gives 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP in the citric acid cycle: 3(2.5) + 1.5 + 1 = 10 ATP.
x: This puts FADH₂ above NADH. FADH₂ passes its electrons in after complex I, so fewer H⁺ are pumped and fewer ATP form.
This puts one NADH above a whole acetyl CoA. One turn of the citric acid cycle makes 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂ and 1 GTP, far more than one NADH.
This puts acetyl CoA lowest. Each acetyl CoA feeds several NADH and an FADH₂ into the chain, so it yields the most ATP.

q: Compounds I–III all have a molar mass of about 74 g/mol. Rank them from lowest to highest boiling point.
h: With similar masses, compare the attractions between molecules: which have no O–H, one O–H, or an O–H plus a C=O?
w: III < II < I. Diethyl ether (III, 35 °C) has no O–H, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other. 1-Butanol (II, 118 °C) hydrogen bonds through its O–H. Propanoic acid (I, 141 °C) boils highest because pairs of acid molecules hold together by two hydrogen bonds (C=O to O–H both ways).
x: Diethyl ether is placed above 1-butanol here. The ether has no O–H, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other.
1-Butanol is placed above propanoic acid here. Carboxylic acid molecules pair up through two hydrogen bonds, so the acid boils above an alcohol of the same mass.
This order is reversed. The ether has the weakest attractions between its molecules, so it boils lowest.

q:
Which statements about solubility in water are true?
I. 1-Pentanol is less soluble in water than ethanol.
II. Hexane does not dissolve in water because it cannot hydrogen bond with water.
III. Acetone dissolves in water because water's O–H hydrogen bonds to acetone's C=O oxygen.
h: Compare the polar part and the nonpolar part of each molecule, and ask whether it can hydrogen bond with water.
w: I, II and III. I is true: 1-pentanol's longer nonpolar chain outweighs its one –OH, while ethanol mixes with water in all proportions. II is true: hexane has only C–H bonds, cannot hydrogen bond with water and forms a separate layer. III is true: acetone has no O–H of its own, but the lone pairs on its C=O oxygen accept hydrogen bonds from water.
x: Statement III is true. Acetone's C=O oxygen has lone pairs that accept hydrogen bonds from water.
Statement II is true. Hexane has only C–H bonds, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water and stays as a separate layer.
Statement I is true. The longer nonpolar chain of 1-pentanol makes it less soluble than ethanol, which mixes with water in all proportions.

q: Which of alkenes I–III can exist as cis and trans isomers?
h: Look at each carbon of the C=C. Cis–trans isomers need two different groups on both of those carbons.
w: III only. In 2-pentene (III), one C=C carbon holds H and CH3 and the other holds H and CH2CH3, so cis and trans forms exist. 1-Butene (I) has a CH2= end carbon with two identical H atoms. 2-Methylpropene (II) has two H on one C=C carbon and two CH3 on the other.
x: Compound I cannot. Its end carbon is CH₂=, with two identical H atoms.
Compound II cannot. Each carbon of its double bond has two identical groups.
Compound II cannot. One carbon of its C=C holds two CH₃ groups, so swapping sides gives the same molecule.
